title: Review: Stereophonic in London's West End

I really wanted to see Stereophonic because well it holds the record for the number of Tony nominations for a play and it won the award for best play. So I was drawn to it like a moth to a flame. But in this case, the blame was that I have no interest in rock music, uh, let alone the factory that produces the sausage. Once this three-hour play began, I soon remembered that it was not likely to be my sniff of cocaine. So, how did I get on with the story of a rock band spending a year in a recording studio? I'm Paul 7 Lewis and in these reviews I try to tell you what the show is about uh what the production looks like and how good the acting is. so distonic. If the uh Amazon Prime drama series Daisy Jones and the Sixth or Get Back, the 8-hour trilogy of films documenting the Beatles recording of Let It Be wetted your appetite for delving into the Babylon of the 1970s that gave birth to some of our greatest popular music, then this will be the show for you. Of course, if after seeing that you've had enough of that, that's a different story. For me, the interminable conversations between the various band members about their relationships and about the recording that made up the first half of this show were only alleviated really by the songs themselves. Uh, written by Will Butler, formerly of Arcade Fire, they're actually pretty good pastiches of 70s rock and uh, very nice to listen to. And to be fair, there was some witty dialogue from the author of the play, David Ame. The unnecessarily long first half sets up a much more interesting second half. As relationships break up, uh, tensions between the band rise, and questions are raised about the nature of creativity, the play becomes more and more gripping. Here's the plot. It's the mid 1970s. A rock band are recording their second album. The five members are a mix of British and Americans. Um, and they comprise two couples plus the drummer. As they begin work in the studio, uh, word comes through that a single from their first album and then the album itself are climbing the charts. Suddenly, much more money is made available to them by the record company. And this turns out to be a case of be careful what you wish for because without the discipline of a time limit, paranoia and perfectionism run unbridled. And the recording extends in length to a whole year. The entire play written in four acts takes place in the studio. So we as an audience feel as trapped as the band in this cramped timeless space reminiscent of a scenario by Samuel Beckett. Um three hours of repetition with the same seven phases start to seem like a year. Designed by David Zinn, the set is constructed in meticulous detail with a recording booth uh behind glass at the back of the stage and the sound desk and relaxation area at the front. The most interesting character is the band leader and driving force, Peter, given an edgy performance by Jack Rutterford. It's a stunning portrayal of an artistic genius never satisfied with the quality of the work. His increasingly controlling nature combined with an absence of social skills annoys all those present. He combines long silences, lack of consultation, and cutting criticism with a selfcentered unawareness of his effect on others. In particular, he picks on his longtime girlfriend Diana, played by Lucy Kacheski. Not entirely coincidentally, she has written their hit single and is contributing as many songs as him to the new album. So whether it's professional jealousy or his desire to dominate her, he deliberately undermines her confidence in both her writing and singing, which leads to an increasingly fraught relationship. Zachary Hart gives life to bass player Regge. His brain is so addled with alcohol, he can hardly put one foot in front of the other. But he can still lay down a great baseline. His behavior is to the detriment of his relationship with his wife, who's also the band's keyboard player, Holly, played by Nia Tao. As he begins to replace his addiction to drink with new addictions to various forms of lifestyle and philosophy, he becomes quite humorously a proletizer looking to button hole and bore anyone he meets with his new age beliefs. Simon, the drummer, who founded the band, has been away from his family for far too long. And while he seems like the level-headed one, he too is subject to moments of ego and insecurity. Chris Stack cleverly adopts a calm, slightly strangulated advice that hides his character's anxieties. And we also see why common sense like his will not get the best out of this creative process. The two women are not respected by the man despite the quality of their work. And ironically, they seem unde underdeveloped as characters in this play. Their generally downto-earth behavior and attitudes with occasional tears and shouting hints at their troubled lives rather than revealing what drives them. And this especially applies to Diana whose talent for writing appears to come from nowhere in the context of the play. And while her lack of confidence turns out to be more the product of her destructive relationship with Peter, we get little insight into how she would get into or get out of it. Trying to hold things together is the recording engineer Grover. A masterful portrait of nerves, obsequiousness, and frustration from Eli Gelb. His hapless assistant Charlie, played by Andrew R. Butler, provides much needed light relief. And like Chris Stack, these two are from the original Broadway cast. Now, I don't want to give the impression that it's all argument and mental breakdown. There is also humor in the bickering and banter uh of David Ame's natural sounding conversations. Eventually the album is finished but the battle to produce it has left many casualties. I felt like one of them. However, the second act goes a long way to redeeming the first. I think how highly you rate this play may depend on your interest in the subject matter because unlike say Dear England and its study of leadership in a football setting, stereophonic study of the creative process doesn't take you far enough beyond its rock music context. So, I give Stereophonic three stars. I hope you found this review useful, if not enjoyable. And uh if you did, please like, comment, and uh subscribe to this channel.
